dm: The element of space in the eastern direction and the southern direction, And likewise in the western direction and the northern direction, is infinite; It exists above, below, and in all the ten directions as far as they extend. It is without differentiation and without any distinctions.
gm: The element of space in the eastern direction and the southern direction, And likewise in the western direction and the northern direction, is boundless; Above, below, and in as many of the ten directions as there are, it exists; There is no difference and there is no distinction.

dm: The suchness of the past, the suchness of the future, The suchness of the present, and the suchness of the Arhats, The suchness of all phenomena, and the suchness of the Victors— This suchness of phenomena is entirely without distinction.
gm: Whatever is the suchness of the past, the suchness of the future, Whatever is the suchness of the present, the suchness of an arhat, Whatever is the suchness of all dharmas, the suchness of a Victor— All this suchness of dharmas is without distinction.

dm: The awakening of the Sugatas is free from any differentiation of phenomena; Any bodhisattva who wishes to attain this, If they lack the wisdom of the Guides endowed with skillful means, will not attain it.
gm: The enlightenment of the Sugatas is free from differentiated dharmas; Any bodhisattva who desires to attain this, Even if endowed with skillful means, will not attain it without the guiding wisdom of the perfection of wisdom.

dm: Just as a bird with a massive body of one hundred and fifty yojanas, If its wings are exhausted and it lacks strength and skill, Even if it leaps from the Abode of the Thirty-Three to this world of Jambudvīpa, It will surely meet with disaster and ruin.
gm: If a bird with a large body of one hundred and fifty yojanas, Whose wings are worn out, lacks strength and skill, And jumps from the abode of the Thirty-Three to this Jambudvīpa, In jumping itself, it will come to ruin there.

dm: Even if these five perfections of the Victors were practiced For many tens of billions of eons, And one constantly relied upon infinite and vast aspirations within the world, Without skillful means and separated from wisdom, one falls into the level of a śrāvaka.
gm: Even if these five perfections of the Victors Have been accomplished for many koṭis of niyutas of eons, And one has constantly relied on the world with boundless, vast aspirations, Lacking skillful means and devoid of wisdom, one will fall into the level of a śrāvaka.

dm: Whoever wishes to set forth in this Buddha vehicle Should train with an even mind toward all beings, the recognition of them as parents, A helpful attitude, and a loving heart, Being without harshness, remaining straightforward, and speaking gentle words.
gm: Whoever desires to definitely emerge in this vehicle of the Buddha, With an even mind toward all beings, perceiving them as parents, Should act with an attitude of benefit and a mind of loving-kindness, Be free from rigidity, straightforward, and speak gentle words.

dm: Thus did the elder Subhūti request of the Protector of the World: "Please explain the signs of the ocean of qualities free from afflictions, And how those of great power do not turn back; O Victor, please grant a prophecy regarding even a mere portion of such qualities."
gm: The elder Subhūti thoroughly requested the Protector of the World: "Ocean of Qualities, please teach the signs of those free from afflictions. How those of great power will not turn back again— Thus, may the Victor explain just a fraction of their qualities."

dm: They are free from the perception of diversity and speak words consistent with reason; They do not rely on other śramaṇas or brahmins. These wise ones have forever abandoned the three lower realms; They are intensely devoted to the paths of the ten virtuous actions.
gm: Free from differentiated perceptions and speaking rational words, Not relying on other śramaṇas and brahmins; The wise always abandon the three lower realms at all times, And vividly strive in the path of the ten virtuous actions.

dm: They teach the Dharma to beings without any regard for material gain. They take singular delight in the Dharma and always speak with gentle words. They possess constant alertness while moving, walking, sleeping, and sitting. They walk while looking only a yoke-length ahead, keeping the mind free from delusion.
gm: Without material motives, they subsequently teach the dharma to beings. Singly rejoicing in the dharma, they are always endowed with gentle words. They are fully endowed with clear comprehension when going, walking, sleeping, and sitting. Looking ahead only the distance of a yoke, they walk without a wandering mind.

dm: Pure and wearing clean robes, they are pure in the three isolations; They do not desire gain, and like great bulls, they always long for the Dharma. They have transcended the realm of Māra and are not dependent on others; They meditate on the four concentrations, yet do not dwell within those concentrations.
gm: Making themselves clean and wearing clean clothes, the three are isolated and pure; Without desire for gain, the supreme leaders always desire the dharma. Passed beyond the realm of Māra and not placing themselves under the control of others, Meditating on the four dhyānas, they do not abide in those dhyānas.

dm: They do not desire fame, and their minds are not entangled by anger. Even if they live as householders, they are always without attachment to any material things. For the sake of their livelihood, they do not seek out vast possessions. They do not practice wrathful spells of violence, nor do they practice spells for union with women.
gm: Not desiring fame, their minds are not wrapped by anger. Even if they are householders, they are always unattached to all things. For the sake of livelihood, they do not seek resources through appalling means. They do not practice mantras of fierce actions, nor mantras for uniting men and women.

dm: They do not act as diviners, predicting whether those engaged in desire will have a boy or a girl. They strive in the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is utterly secluded, free from strife and contention, and their minds of loving-kindness are firm. Desiring omniscience, they are steadfast and possess a mind constantly dedicated to it.
gm: They do not predict, saying, 'You will become a man or a woman engaged in actions of desire.' In the utterly isolated perfection of wisdom, they are free from conflict and dispute, and their mind of loving-kindness is firm. Desiring omniscience, they are steadfast and always endowed with a mind inclined toward it.

dm: They have completely avoided the borderlands and the regions of barbarian peoples. They are never uncertain about their own stage, remaining as steadfast as Mount Meru. They would even sacrifice their lives for the sake of the Dharma and are devoted to the diligence of yoga. One should know that these are the signs of the state of non-retrogression.
gm: They completely abandon the borderlands of uncivilized border-dwellers. Without self-doubt, they are always like Mount Sumeru. Giving up even their lives for the sake of the dharma, they vividly strive in yoga. One should know that these are the signs of an irreversible one.

dm: Form, feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness, Are profound, by nature signless, and utterly peaceful. Just as one might seek to reach the bottom of the ocean with an arrow, When analyzed with wisdom, the depth of the aggregates cannot be found.
gm: Form, feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness Are profound, naturally signless, and utterly peaceful; For example, like searching for the bottom of the ocean with an arrow, When examined with wisdom, the depth of the aggregates cannot be found.

dm: Any bodhisattva who has become profound in that way, And who realizes this Dharma—the ultimate, unattached vehicle in which aggregates, Elements, and sense sources do not exist— What could there be that is a more perfect accomplishment of merit than that?
gm: For any bodhisattva who realizes this profound Vehicle, ultimate and unattached, wherein the aggregates, Elements, and sense-sources do not exist— What perfectly accomplished merit is there beyond that?

dm: For example, consider a man who indulges in desire and, Having made an appointment with a woman, fails to meet her; However many conceptual thoughts he experiences in his mind throughout a single day, For that many eons, the bodhisattva will achieve attainment.
gm: For example, a man who engages in the phenomena of desire, Having made an appointment with a woman and not meeting her, However many discursive thoughts of his mind operate in a single day, The bodhisattva will gain that many eons.

dm: Any bodhisattva who, for many billions of eons, Practices generosity toward Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas and maintains ethical discipline, Cannot match the merit of one who speaks of the Dharma that possesses the supreme perfection of wisdom, Even if that merit from giving and morality were spoken of well.
gm: Even if a bodhisattva, for many thousands of millions of eons, Gives gifts to arhats and pratyekabuddhas and observes ethical discipline, For anyone who teaches the dharma endowed with the supreme perfection of wisdom, Giving and ethical discipline do not bear a fraction of the goodness of that teaching.

dm: Any bodhisattva who meditates on the supreme perfection of wisdom, And having arisen from that, teaches the stainless Dharma, And dedicates that for the sake of beings as the cause of enlightenment— There is no virtue in the three worlds equal to that.
gm: Any bodhisattva who meditates on the supreme wisdom, Arising from that, teaches the untainted dharma, And dedicates that as a cause for awakening for the sake of beings, There is no virtue equal to that in the three worlds.

dm: Know that such merit is also accumulated, and likewise empty, Hollow, insubstantial, and without essence. When one practices the wisdom of the Sugatas in that manner, At the time of practicing, one fully grasps immeasurable merit.
gm: Knowing that merit, too, to be an accumulation and likewise empty, Hollow, baseless, and coreless— If one thus engages in the wisdom practice of the sugatas, While engaging, one fully grasps immeasurable merit.

dm: Knowing that all these dharmas, which the Buddha has thoroughly practiced and clearly taught, Are exhausted as mere expressions, Even if one were to speak of them for many tens of billions of eons, The expanse of phenomena is without exhaustion and without increase.
gm: Spoken by the Buddha, vividly practiced and vividly taught, Knowing all these dharmas to be nothing more than mere expressions, Even if they are expressed for many tens of millions and hundreds of billions of eons, In the dharmadhātu, there is no depletion and no increase.

dm: Whatever is called the perfection of the Victors, Those phenomena are also proclaimed to be merely names. A bodhisattva who dedicates without conceptual arrogance Will not decline and will touch the supreme awakening of a Buddha.
gm: Whatever is called the perfection of the victors, Those dharmas too are fully proclaimed to be merely names. A bodhisattva who fully dedicates without a conceited mind Will without decline touch the supreme awakening of a buddha.

dm: Just as when a lamp is lit, the wick is not consumed by the first encounter with the flame, The wick is not the flame, yet without it, the flame does not burn; The wick is not burned by its final contact with the flame, Just as without that final flame, the wick is not burned.
gm: By the first contact of the burning wick of an oil lamp, The wick is not burned, yet without it, it is not burned. By the final contact of the flame, the wick is not burned, Yet without the final flame, the wick is not burned—just as,

dm: Supreme enlightenment is not reached by the initial mind, Yet without that initial mind, it cannot be reached. Peaceful enlightenment is not attained by the final mind, Yet without that, it is also impossible to attain it.
gm: By the first mind, supreme awakening is not touched, Yet without it, one is not able to touch it. By the final mind, peaceful awakening is not attained, Yet without it, one is not able to attain it.

dm: From a seed, the sprout, flower, and fruit arise; Just as it is not the case that the tree does not exist because the seed has ceased, So too, the initial mind is the cause of awakening; It is not the case that awakening does not exist because that mind has ceased.
gm: From a seed, a sprout, a flower, and a fruit arise, And when it ceases, the tree is not absent there—just as, Likewise, the first mind is also the cause of awakening, And when it ceases, it is not that awakening is absent.

dm: Just as a water jar is gradually filled from the first drop to the last, Little by little, it is completely filled; So too, the initial mind is the cause of supreme enlightenment, And by gradually perfecting virtuous qualities, one becomes a Buddha.
gm: By drops of water, a vase from the first to the last, Is gradually, little by little, fully filled—just as, Likewise, the first mind too is the cause of supreme awakening, Gradually, perfecting white virtues, one becomes a buddha.
